title: Count Coin Combinations
statement:
You get an integer amount and a list coins of distinct coin values. You have an unlimited supply of every coin.

Return how many different combinations of coins add up to exactly amount. Order does not matter: 2 + 5 and 5 + 2 are the same combination. Two combinations differ only if some coin value is used a different number of times. For amount = 0 the empty combination counts, so the answer is 1.

examples.why: 5 + 2 and 3 + 2 + 2. Counting orders instead would give 5: two for 5 + 2 and three for 3 + 2 + 2.
Taking no coins at all is one way to make 0.

constraints: The answer fits in a signed 32-bit integer
hints: To count each combination once, fix an order in which coins are decided: first how many of coin 0, then how many of coin 1, and so on.

Let dp[i][x] be the number of ways to make x using only the first i coin values. For coin i, either you use none of it, or you use at least one, which leaves x − c to make with the same coins still allowed.
dp[i][x] = dp[i−1][x] + dp[i][x − c]. In one array: loop over coins on the outside and amounts upward on the inside, doing ways[x] += ways[x − c]. Swapping the loops counts orders instead.

explain.intuition:
The trap is counting 2 + 5 and 5 + 2 twice. The cure is to decide coins in a fixed order, one value at a time. Let dp[i][x] be the number of combinations that make x using only the first i coin values. Read it off the last decision, about coin c = coins[i−1]: either the combination uses no c, giving dp[i−1][x], or it uses at least one. Take one away and you have a combination of x − c that may still use c again, giving dp[i][x − c]. The two groups do not overlap and together cover everything, so dp[i][x] = dp[i−1][x] + dp[i][x − c], with dp[0][0] = 1 and dp[0][x > 0] = 0.

Row i reads only row i−1 at the same x and its own row further left, so one array works: for each coin, sweep x upward and do ways[x] += ways[x − c]. The loop order is the whole point. With coins outside, each combination is built in one fixed coin order and is counted once. With amounts outside and coins inside, ways[x] asks "which coin was added last?", and that counts every ordering, 5 instead of 2 in the first example.
steps: For x from c up to amount: ways[x] += ways[x − c]. Going upward lets ways[x − c] already include this coin, so it can be used many times.
pitfalls: Putting the amount loop outside and the coin loop inside. That counts sequences, so amount = 7, coins = [5, 2, 3] gives 5 instead of 2.
Sweeping x downward. That is the "each coin at most once" version and answers 1 instead of 2 for amount = 9, coins = [3, 9].
Starting with ways[0] = 0. Every count is built from the empty combination; without it everything stays 0.

solutions.title: Recursion: use this coin again, or move past it
solutions.idea: f(i, rest): either take one more coins[i] and stay at i, or never use coins[i] again and move to i + 1. Moving forward only is what stops reorderings. No memory, so it repeats work.

solutions.title: Table of coins × amounts
solutions.idea: dp[i][x] = dp[i−1][x] (no coin i) + dp[i][x − c] (at least one coin i).

solutions.title: One array, coins on the outside
solutions.idea: Sweep amounts upward once per coin: ways[x] += ways[x − c]. The coin loop must be the outer one.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def countCombos(self, amount: int, coins: List[int]) -> int:
        ways = [1] + [0] * amount
        for c in coins:                      # coins outside: each combination counted once
            for x in range(c, amount + 1):   # upward: this coin may repeat
                ways[x] += ways[x - c]
        return ways[amount]

followups: Count ordered sequences instead (5 + 2 and 2 + 5 differ). Which loop goes outside now?
Each coin value may be used at most once. What single change makes that work in the one-array version?
Return the fewest coins that make the amount instead of the number of combinations.
